traveler: Odoric of Pordenone (Odorico Mattiussi, beato Odorico da Pordenone)
title: The Relatio: Friuli to Khanbaliq and the Island of the Dog-Faced Men
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Villanova di Pordenone, birth in the Patriarchate
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. Treccani (Andrea Tilatti, DBI 79, 2013) says only Pordenone; the hamlet of Villanova is traditional attribution, correctly hedged. The year c. 1280 rests on a 2002 forensic examination of the partly mummified remains, which indicated a man of about fifty at death, and displaces the older proposals of 1265, 1274/75 and 1286. The Minor Planet Center naming citation for asteroid 4637 still prints 1265. Month and day are unknown and defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: A son is born in the Patriarchate of Aquileia, in or near the hamlet of Villanova, a walk from the walls of Pordenone. The family name later given him is Mattiussi; the town's name is the one that travels. He enters a Friuli of notaries, castles and small ecclesiastical lordships, a country where every fact about a man is a parchment somebody kept. Almost nothing of the childhood survives that treatment. What survives instead is a body, examined in Udine in 2002, partly mummified, about fifty years old at death, which sets the birth here and not fifteen years earlier.
suggested_refs: The traditional birth house at Villanova di Pordenone
The 2002 diocesan forensic examination of the remains at Udine
sources: Andrea Tilatti, 'Odorico da Pordenone,' Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani 79 (2013), treccani.it

stops.name: Gemona del Friuli, a boy among the Friars Minor
stops.date_confidence: Act attested, identification contested. Treccani confirms the date, the place and the phrase verbatim: an act at Gemona del Friuli on 9 February 1296 naming an Odolricus puer fratrum Minorum. Tilatti calls the identification with the traveler attractive but not certain, so the claim is carried here as [R]. The research pool's two lenses disagree on the tag, one [A] and one [R], and the count of five friar-witnesses appears in one lens only and could not be sourced to Treccani.
stops.campa: A notary at Gemona del Friuli draws up an act and lists among the witnesses one Odolricus puer fratrum Minorum, a boy of the Friars Minor. There is a Franciscan house in this Friulian market town and a child already inside the order; that much the parchment establishes, along with the names of the men standing in the room. Whether the child is the man who will reach Khanbaliq, Tilatti will not say. The act gives no second name and no father's name, and twenty years pass before another document names an Odoric at all. The notary had no reason to write down which one he meant. Is it the same boy?
stops.quote_source: Notarial act, Gemona del Friuli, 9 February 1296, as cited in Andrea Tilatti, 'Odorico da Pordenone,' DBI 79 (2013)
suggested_refs: The Franciscan house at Gemona del Friuli
Tilatti's discussion of the 1296 act and its contested identification

stops.name: Cividale del Friuli, named in a notary's act
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year by Treccani, which reports a notarial act of 1316 at Cividale naming Odoric alive as witness or party. Month and day are not given and are defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Cividale, the old Lombard capital on the Natisone, keeps its notaries busy, and in 1316 one of them writes Odoric's name into an act as witness or party. He is roughly thirty-six. He is not a hermit and he is not yet a traveler; he is a friar whom the legal machinery of the Patriarchate finds credible enough to name in front of other men. Somebody wanted his presence on the record and paid a notary to fix it there. The Relatio he will dictate fourteen years later says nothing whatever about these years, or about this town.
suggested_refs: The notarial archives of Cividale del Friuli

stops.name: Porpetto, the castle and the witness list
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year by Treccani: a notarial act of 1317 places Odoric alive at the castle of Porpetto. Month and day defaulted to 01-01. Coordinates corrected: the research pool gave 45.7867, 13.2733, which falls some 9.5 km south-east of the comune toward the Marano lagoon; the pin used here is the Chiesa di San Francesco in the Castello locality of Porpetto, 45.8699, 13.2217, per Nominatim.
stops.campa: At the castle of Porpetto, south toward the lagoon country, his name enters a second act. Three notarial appearances in three consecutive years, in three different towns, describe a man circulating through the province on the order's business: preaching, witnessing, arbitrating, the ordinary work of a Friar Minor in a country of small lordships. Later hagiography will want a hermit in the Friulian woods, living on bread and water, and will supply one. What Porpetto records is duller and firmer: a friar standing in a room in a castle while a notary writes his name down.
suggested_refs: The Castello di Porpetto and the church of San Francesco in its locality

stops.name: Portogruaro, the last European record
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year by Treccani: a notarial act of 1318 at Portogruaro. Month and day defaulted to 01-01. This is the last securely dated European appearance before the journey.
stops.campa: Portogruaro on the Lemene is the last securely dated appearance in Europe. After this act the Friulian record closes, and it does not open again for eleven or twelve years. Between this parchment and the next European document that names him lies the whole journey: Persia, the Malabar coast, the islands, Cathay, the road back overland. Nothing in the act suggests a departure. It is a friar witnessing a piece of business in a river town, and then the province stops writing his name down. Nobody recorded why he left, or whether anyone in Portogruaro knew he was going.
suggested_refs: The notarial record of Portogruaro, 1318

stops.name: Venice, the departure that cannot be dated
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed. Tilatti holds that the departure is best placed after 1318; the older chronologies proposing 1316 or 1317 lack traceable authority. The Relatio gives elapsed travel time and never a calendar date, so no day, month or ship can be fixed. Coordinates corrected: the pool's 45.4342, 12.3388 sits on nineteenth-century landfill at Sant'Elena; the pin used is the Bacino di San Marco waterfront, 45.4330, 12.3410.
stops.campa: He goes down to Venice and takes ship for the Black Sea. No document gives the day, the vessel or the company; the Relatio counts elapsed time and never a calendar date, so the departure can be fixed only as later than the act at Portogruaro. Venice is the gate: galleys running to Trebizond, Franciscan houses strung along the caravan roads beyond, and a Mongol peace that has made the whole line passable for a man on foot with a licence. What he says he is going for, he says at the start of the book, in the first person and without ornament.
stops.quote: ALBEIT many other stories of sundry kinds concerning the customs and peculiarities of different parts of this world have been related by a variety of persons, yet would I have you to know that I also, Friar Odoric of Friuli, can truly rehearse many great marvels which I did hear and see when, according to my wish, I crossed the sea and visited the countries of the unbelievers in order to win some harvest of souls.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Friar Odoric, ch. 1, in Henry Yule (trans.), rev. Henri Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (Hakluyt Society, 1913), p. 97
suggested_refs: The Venetian galley line to Trebizond in the early fourteenth century
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Constantinople, passed without description
stops.date_confidence: Reconstructed from the Relatio's route notices; the text supplies no date and Yule's chapter sequence supplies only order. The year here is an ordering device, not a documented year.
stops.campa: The route passes Constantinople, the standard staging post for friars bound east, and the Relatio gives it almost nothing: no emperor, no Hagia Sophia, no marvel worth a paragraph. Odoric's attention does not switch on until the road turns strange. He is not writing a pilgrimage and he is not writing a chronicle; he is writing down what he judges the brothers at home will not already know from merchants and letters. A city with a Latin quarter and a Venetian dock fails that test and gets a line. Whether he stayed a night there or a season, the text does not say.
suggested_refs: The Genoese quarter at Pera and the Latin houses of Constantinople, staging posts of the eastern mission
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Trebizond, where the caravan road begins
stops.date_confidence: Place attested by the Relatio's own first chapter, which is headed 'What the Friar saw at Trebizond and in the Greater Armenia'. The date is not. A widely repeated 1317 arrival traces to d'Avezac and has no traceable authority; the 1319 used here is an ordering device only. Canonical corpus pin, inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: At Trebizond the sea road ends and the caravan road begins, and here the first chapter of the Relatio opens. He notes the trade of the port, the goods coming up out of Persia, the Greek despotate holding its stretch of coast. Older reference works give him an arrival in 1317; that year traces back to d'Avezac and rests on nothing anyone can produce. What the text supplies instead is a starting line. From this harbour a friar in grey walks inland toward Armenia, and from here the marvels begin to accumulate at the pace of the road.
suggested_refs: The Black Sea terminus of the Persian caravan road at Trebizond
Yule-Cordier's chapter 1, 'What the Friar saw at Trebizond and in the Greater Armenia'
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Erzurum, the years Yule could not account for
stops.date_confidence: Place named in the Relatio as Arziron; the date is an ordering device. Yule's suggestion that unexplained years before 1322 were spent in Franciscan houses along this corridor is his inference and not Odoric's testimony, and is carried here as such.
stops.campa: Arziron in the text, Erzurum on a modern map, sits on the Anatolian plateau where the caravan road climbs toward the Persian frontier. The Relatio gives it a sentence and goes on. Yule, editing the text six centuries later, noticed that the chronology has years in it that nothing accounts for, and guessed the friar spent some of them in the Franciscan houses along this corridor, learning the languages he would need further east. Odoric never says anything of the kind. The guess is Yule's, printed in Yule's footnote, and the years are still unaccounted for.
suggested_refs: Yule-Cordier's editorial note on the unaccounted years before 1322
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Tabriz, inside the Mongol peace
stops.date_confidence: Place attested in the Relatio as Tauris; the date is an ordering device. The presence of a Franciscan convent at Tabriz in this period is documented, but no source places Odoric inside it, and the shelter is offered here as possibility only.
stops.campa: Tauris, which is Tabriz, is the great trading capital of the Ilkhanate, and the Relatio marks its wealth. Caravans out of Genoa and out of India unload in the same streets. He is inside the Mongol peace now, and to a man on foot that peace is not an abstraction: it is a road with lodging on it, letters that travel along it, and men in grey habits at the far end of a month's walking who will feed another man in a grey habit. A Franciscan convent stood in Tabriz in these years. Whether Odoric slept in it, no source says.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan convent at Tabriz under the Ilkhanate
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Soltaniyeh, the capital still being built
stops.date_confidence: Place attested in the Relatio as Soldania; the date is an ordering device. The Latin archbishopric of Soltaniyeh, erected in 1318 for the eastern mission field, is documented independently of Odoric.
stops.campa: Soldania is new, still going up: the Ilkhan's capital raised on the summer pastures, and over the royal tomb a dome among the largest in brick ever attempted. Rome erected an archbishopric here in 1318, the administrative head of the whole eastern mission field, and Odoric walks through the machinery his own journey depends on. The Relatio records the city. It records nothing of what he was told in the archbishop's house, or by whom. He is a passing friar from Friuli in a capital built for somebody else, and the book moves him south.
suggested_refs: The Latin archbishopric of Soltaniyeh, erected 1318
The mausoleum of Oljeitu at Soltaniyeh
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Kashan, a name in the sequence
stops.date_confidence: Place named in Yule's chapter sequence as Cassan; the date is an ordering device. Yule inserts Cassan, Yezd, Comerum and Chaldaea between Soldania and Ormes, and no two editors agree on what that sequence means as an itinerary on the ground.
stops.campa: Cassan, in Yule's chapter order, comes after Soldania on the road south. The Relatio names it and gives the reader almost nothing else. Between here and the Gulf the manuscript sequence runs Kashan, Yazd, Comerum, Chaldaea, then Hormuz, and no two editors have agreed on what that order means as a route across the Iranian plateau. He is crossing it in stages a caravan would recognise, on a road with wells on it and stopping places other men keep. Months of walking go into the text as a clause. That is how the whole book is built.
suggested_refs: Yule-Cordier's chapter sequence between Soldania and Ormes
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Yazd, at the edge of the salt desert
stops.date_confidence: Place named in the Relatio as Yezd; the date is an ordering device with no documentary basis.
stops.campa: Yezd sits at the edge of the salt desert, a city of wind towers and underground water channels, and the friar passes through it southbound. He is now two or three years out of Friuli by any reconstruction, and no reconstruction can prove which. The method of the Relatio is clear by this point: a place is named when something in it is worth carrying home, and skipped when it is only distance to be got over. Yazd gets a name and a line, and beyond the last of its houses the salt.
suggested_refs: The qanat system and wind towers of Yazd
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Persepolis, ruins without a vocabulary
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The account describes ruins that editors have identified with Persepolis; the identification is Tilatti's and Yule's, not Odoric's, and whether he saw the terrace or was told about it on the road the text does not settle. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The account describes great ruins in the Persian south, and editors have identified them with Persepolis, the burned palace of Darius and Xerxes standing open on its terrace above the plain. Whether Odoric walked that terrace or heard it described by a caravan man, the text does not settle and the editors do not pretend it does. A Franciscan from Friuli stands in front of Achaemenid columns, or listens to somebody describe them, with no word available to him for what he is looking at except the word for ruins.
suggested_refs: The terrace of Persepolis, identified by Yule and Tilatti with the ruins of the Relatio
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Baghdad, the reconstructed bend
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and Tilatti says so: the route is reconstructed through Baghdad and lower Mesopotamia toward the Gulf, but the account's ordering of this stretch is not secure. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The reconstructed route bends through Baghdad and down the Mesopotamian rivers toward the Gulf. Sixty years after Hulagu took it, the city is a provincial capital of the Ilkhanate and no longer the seat of the caliphs. The Relatio's ordering of this whole stretch is loose enough that Tilatti will call the passage probable and leave it there. Odoric is somewhere in lower Mesopotamia, moving toward salt water on roads and rivers that other men maintain, and the text has stopped keeping count of the days.
suggested_refs: Tilatti's caution on the insecure ordering of the Mesopotamian stretch

stops.name: Hormuz, aboard other men's ships
stops.date_confidence: Place attested in the Relatio as Ormes; the date is an ordering device. That Odoric traveled by ordinary merchant shipping rather than any dedicated expedition is Tilatti's characterisation of the route, supported by the Relatio's own silence about any vessel of his own.
stops.campa: At Ormes on the Gulf he stops walking and starts sailing. What carries him is not an expedition and not a fleet: it is the ordinary Indian Ocean merchant traffic, ships built by other men for other cargoes, which he boards because they are going where he is going. The whole journey works like this, taken in sequence: caravan roads, mendicant houses, Mongol post stations, other men's hulls. He has no funds, no escort and no commission except the one his own order gave him.
suggested_refs: The Indian Ocean merchant shipping network at Hormuz

segments.name: India, and the Bones of the Four

stops.name: Thane, the bones taken up
stops.date_confidence: The martyrdom is attested to 8 April 1321 (some Franciscan martyrologies give 9 April) and is used here as the segment's anchor and the journey's firm terminus post quem; Odoric arrives afterward, at an interval no source measures. Two corrections to the research pool: Demetrius of Tiflis was a lay interpreter, not a friar, and Yule's chapter 13 is headed 'How Fr. Odoric took up the bones of the four friars', so the pool's exclusion of Peter of Siena's body is wrong. Coordinates corrected from 19.1972, 72.9722 to the town centre.
stops.campa: He comes ashore at Tana and what he finds is a fresh grave. In April four men of his own world were killed here after a dispute before a Muslim judge: the Franciscans Thomas of Tolentino, James of Padua and Peter of Siena, and Demetrius of Tiflis, a layman who served them as interpreter. Peter was killed three days after the others. Odoric takes up the bones of all four, and from this point he is carrying them. The relics cross the Bay of Bengal with him and go on into China. His journey now has a cargo and a reason that is not curiosity.
suggested_refs: Yule-Cordier ch. 13, 'How Fr. Odoric took up the bones of the four friars'
The Franciscan martyrology of the four killed at Tana, April 1321
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), chs. 6-13, archive.org

stops.name: Flandrina, the pepper coast
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Odoric's own form of the name is Flandrina, which Yule identifies with Pandarani, Panthalayani Kollam, modern Koyilandy; Pandarani is the later Portuguese form and Ibn Battuta's is Fandaraina. The year is a reconstruction, not a documented date: the western-India arrival can be dated only to soon after April 1321. Coordinates corrected from 11.17, 75.6, which fell offshore of Beypore some 32 km south.
stops.campa: Flandrina, which Yule identifies with Panthalayani Kollam on the Malabar coast, is a pepper port. Odoric describes the vine climbing its trellises, the gathering, the drying, the trade that brings ships from Arabia and from China to load it. Here his eye is at its best and his prose at its plainest: he counts, he names, he says what a thing is worth and how it is grown. The dog-faced men are two thousand miles ahead of him yet. For now there is pepper going out onto the drying floors, and a friar writing down what it fetches.
suggested_refs: Panthalayani Kollam (Koyilandy), the Flandrina of Odoric and the Fandaraina of Ibn Battuta
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Cranganore, among the Thomas Christians
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Cranganore is named in the coastal itinerary as reconstructed by Yule; the year carries the same reconstruction as the rest of the Malabar leg. That Odoric met Saint Thomas Christians on this coast is inference from the community's documented presence there, not a statement he makes at this stop.
stops.campa: Cranganore, the old spice harbour, is another stop on a coast he treats almost as an inventory: pepper, ginger, coconut, the wine drawn from the palm. The Saint Thomas Christians have been on this shore for centuries, with their own liturgy, their own hierarchy and their own claim to an apostolic founding older than most of Europe's. A Latin friar meeting them has to decide what they are. The Relatio is guarded on the question and accuses nobody of anything, which for a fourteenth-century mendicant is a considered position.
suggested_refs: The Saint Thomas Christian communities of the Malabar coast
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Quilon, everything through interpreters
stops.date_confidence: Place attested; the year is the same Malabar reconstruction. Coordinates corrected from 76.5924, which put the pin about 2.4 km west into the Ashtamudi backwater; the town centre is 8.8932, 76.6141.
stops.campa: Columbum in the text is Quilon, and the account there records local produce and local custom, all of it filtered through interpreters he never names. A man with no Malayalam and no Tamil is told things by men whose own knowledge is often second hand, and he writes down what reaches him in whatever language the two of them share. That is the structural limit of the book. Some of what reaches him is exact to the item and the price. Some of it, four chapters on, will be men with the faces of dogs.
suggested_refs: The port of Kollam in the fourteenth-century pepper trade
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Mylapore, at the apostle's shrine
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Relatio: Odoric visits the shrine of St Thomas the Apostle at Mylapore. The year carries the Malabar-leg reconstruction and is not independently documented.
stops.campa: Near Mylapore he prays at the shrine that holds, by tradition, the body of the apostle Thomas, who is said to have died in India and to have founded the churches Odoric has been walking past for weeks. For a Franciscan a thousand miles beyond the last Latin bishop this is proof that the road he is on was walked before him: the mission field is not new, it is only lapsed. He describes the site and the devotion around it, Christian and otherwise, and does not rule on whose shrine it properly is. Then he takes ship for Ceylon.
suggested_refs: The shrine of St Thomas the Apostle at Mylapore
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Adam's Peak, the mountain of the tears
stops.date_confidence: Place attested in the Relatio as Sillan; the year is reconstruction. Canonical corpus pin for Ceylon and Adam's Peak, inherited byte-identical from the existing atlas entry rather than repinned to the summit of Sri Pada. The chapter's own content mixes direct notice with inherited marvel lore and the paraphrase here follows Yule's chapter, not a verbatim text.
stops.campa: Sillan is Ceylon, and its mountain carries the footprint that three religions claim as their own. Odoric reports the tradition that Adam mourned his son here for a hundred years, and that the lake below the summit is made of his tears. He reports gems in the water, leeches in the grass, and beasts he considers extraordinary. The chapter mixes what a traveller could see with what a traveller is told, and nowhere marks the seam between them. Yule, editing it six hundred years later, marks it for him in the footnotes.
suggested_refs: Sri Pada and the three-faith veneration of the footprint on Adam's Peak
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

segments.name: The Islands of the Marvel Book

stops.name: Lamori, where the pole star goes under
stops.date_confidence: Place attested in the Relatio as Lamori; the year is an ordering device only, since the manuscript order of the Southeast Asian chapters does not form a navigationally coherent route and no source assigns a year to this stretch. Coordinates corrected from 5.25, 97.1, which landed in the north-central Sumatran interior; Lamuri lay in Aceh Besar around Banda Aceh, at Lambaro or Lam Reh.
stops.campa: Lamori is the northern tip of Sumatra and it is where the pole star goes under the horizon. He notices the sky change, which is the observation of a man who was genuinely at sea and watching. Then, in the same breath, he reports that the people go naked, hold their wives in common, and eat human flesh the way Europeans eat beef. The two halves of that chapter sit side by side with no seam between them, and the book supplies its reader with no instrument whatever for telling one half from the other.
stops.quote: It is an evil and a pestilent generation, and they eat man's flesh there just as we eat beef here. Yet the country in itself is excellent, and hath great store of flesh-meats, and of wheat and of rice; and they have much gold also, and lign-aloes, and camphor, and many other things which are produced there.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Friar Odoric, ch. 20 (Lamori), Yule-Cordier trans., Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II, p. 148
suggested_refs: The Lamuri kingdom of Aceh Besar
Yule-Cordier ch. 20, 'Concerning the country called Lamori, where the pole star is hidden'
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Java, a palace no wall answers to
stops.date_confidence: Place attested in the Relatio; the year is an ordering device. The description is not tied to any surviving structure and the pin is a general one for the island's interior court region, not an identified site.
stops.campa: He describes a king of Java rich beyond counting, spices growing in quantities that make the whole European trade look like a rumour of itself, and a palace of a lavishness that no surviving structure answers to. The island is real and its court was real. What stood inside that court cannot be checked against a single standing wall, and this is the register the book keeps sliding into as it moves east through the islands. Did he walk into the palace, or was he told about it in a port?
suggested_refs: The Majapahit court of fourteenth-century Java

stops.name: Champa, the widow on the fire
stops.date_confidence: Place attested in the Relatio as Zampa; the year is an ordering device. Yule's editors footnote the widow-burning notice with nineteenth-century Cham ethnographic parallels, which corroborates the custom's plausibility and not Odoric's presence at any particular burning.
stops.campa: Zampa is the Cham coast of what is now central Vietnam. He records elephants in numbers, a king with many wives and many more children, fish that come ashore in shoals to be taken by hand, and tortoises of great size. Nineteenth-century editors footnote this ethnography with Cham parallels and find him corroborated. He also records that when a married man dies his body is burned and his living wife is burned with it. He states that in one sentence, with no commentary, in a book that elsewhere cannot let a marvel pass without a line of wonder.
stops.quote: When a married man dies in this country his body is burned, and his living wife along with it. For they say that she should go to keep company with her husband in the other world also.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Friar Odoric, ch. 23, Yule-Cordier trans., Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II, p. 166
suggested_refs: Yule-Cordier's footnote on Cham widow-cremation parallels
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Nicoveran, the island of the dog-faced men
stops.date_confidence: The chapter is attested as part of the transmitted medieval text; whether Odoric saw anything of the kind is not established and is not claimed here. Yule and Cordier characterise ch. 24 as an anomalous jumble compounding the name of Nicobar, the conventional Andaman location of dog-heads, a Maabar forehead ornament, a Ceylon ruby and the intra-group justice of Ctesias's ancient cynocephali. The year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Sailing south he comes to an island he calls Nicoveran, where, he writes, the men and the women alike have faces like great dogs. They worship an ox and wear its image in gold on the forehead. Their king carries three hundred pearls on a string, one for each daily prayer, and a ruby a span long that shows like a flame of fire, and he keeps justice, so that all men fare safely through his realm. Yule calls the chapter an anomalous jumble: Nicobar's name, the Andamans' dog-heads, a Maabar ornament, and a ruby lifted out of Marco Polo's Ceylon.
stops.quote: This is a great isle, having a compass of a good 2,000 miles, and both the men and the women there have faces like dogs. And these people worship the ox as their god, wherefore they always wear upon the forehead an ox made of gold or silver, in token that he is their god.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Friar Odoric, ch. 24, Yule-Cordier trans., Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II, p. 169
suggested_refs: Yule-Cordier's editorial notes on ch. 24 and the Ctesias cynocephali tradition
Ratramnus of Corbie's ninth-century letter on whether the cynocephali possess reason
The Coptic and Ethiopian tradition of Saint Christopher the dog-headed
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), ch. 24, archive.org

stops.name: Guangzhou, where the itinerary stops wandering
stops.date_confidence: Place attested in the Relatio as Censcalan or Chin-Kalan. The date is not: Treccani dates the Chinese residence only to a presumed 1322-1325, while English Wikipedia gives three years in China between the opening of 1323 and the close of 1328. The pool's flat 1324 for this stop is unsupported and the year here orders the segment.
stops.campa: He calls the place Censcalan. It is Guangzhou, and it is where the itinerary stops wandering: from here the Relatio runs in a line, coast to canal to capital. He calls the city vast and enters the administered world of the Yuan, where a traveller with the right documents moves a thousand miles on post horses and sleeps in ordered lodgings. The marvels thin out from this page onward. What replaces them is counting. He tallies cities and bridges and boats for readers who have no example of a scale like it.
suggested_refs: The Yuan postal relay system, the yam, and its use by licensed travellers

stops.name: Quanzhou, the relics set down
stops.date_confidence: Place attested; the deposit of the Tana relics at the Franciscan house of Zaiton is attested by Tilatti. The claim that Bishop Andrew of Perugia's 1326 letter from Zayton confirms their reception could NOT be verified: the letter is genuinely 1326 and genuinely from Zayton, but no reachable text of it mentions the Tana relics or Odoric, and Treccani does not cite it for this. That claim is therefore [R] here, not the firmest external date in the itinerary as the pool asserted. Canonical corpus pin, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: At Zaiton the friars have houses, and here Odoric sets down the bones he has carried from Tana across the Bay of Bengal: Thomas of Tolentino, James of Padua, Peter of Siena, Demetrius of Tiflis, dead five years and half the world away from Umbria and Tuscany and Georgia. Bishop Andrew of Perugia is writing letters home from this same city in 1326. Whether Andrew's letter mentions the relics could not be confirmed from any text reached, and the arrival cannot be dated more closely than the years the Franciscan house stood.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan houses at Zayton (Quanzhou) under Bishop Andrew of Perugia
Andrew of Perugia's letter from Zayton, 1326
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Fuzhou, a stage and not a scene
stops.date_confidence: Place attested in the Relatio's coastal sequence; the year orders the segment and is not documented. Treccani gives only the sequence Guangzhou, Quanzhou, Fuzhou, Hangzhou, Nanjing, Yangzhou, Khanbaliq, without dates for the intermediate cities.
stops.campa: Fuzhou, north along the coast, is a stage rather than a scene. He notes the trade and passes on. The China chapters move at the speed of the post roads, and the friar is travelling now as an official traveller travels, with lodging arranged ahead of him and a road maintained under him. He does not describe the administration that makes this possible, because to him it is not strange, only large. Fuzhou gets its trade, its name and a line, and then the road carries him north.
suggested_refs: The Yuan coastal road and relay network of Fujian

stops.name: Hangzhou, the greatest city in the whole world
stops.date_confidence: Attested chapter, undocumented year. The wording matters here: the phrase 'greatest city on earth' belongs to the chapter heading in Yule's edition, while the running text reads 'the greatest city in the whole world'. The research pool spliced the heading's wording into the narrative; the quote below is the corrected running text, ch. 32, pp. 192-193.
stops.campa: Cansay, he writes, means the City of Heaven. He gives its bridges, its waterways, its markets, the food coming in by boat, the paper money changing hands, the sheer count of things. It is the most detailed chapter in the book and the one most often cited as evidence that whoever wrote the Relatio was actually standing in China. Yule's chapter heading calls it the greatest city on earth, and editors have been quoting the heading as though it were the narrative. The running text says something slightly different: 'tis the greatest city in the whole world.
stops.quote: Departing thence, I came unto the city of Cansay, a name which signifieth 'the City of Heaven.' And 'tis the greatest city in the whole world.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Friar Odoric, ch. 32, Yule-Cordier trans., Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II, pp. 192-193
suggested_refs: Yule-Cordier ch. 32 on Cansay, and the divergence between its heading and its running text
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Nanjing, counting the Jiangnan
stops.date_confidence: Place attested in Treccani's reconstruction of the China itinerary; the year orders the segment and has no documentary basis.
stops.campa: The route turns inland to the rivers. Nanjing on the Yangtze is a name in a list, one of the cities of the Jiangnan that Treccani's reconstruction has him counting off as he passes, and the counting is the point of it. No chapter stops here. He is trying to make a European reader believe in a density of settlement for which Europe offers no example at all, and the only instrument he has for it is number: so many households, so many boats, so many towns in a day on the water. The Relatio's China is not marvellous. It is populous.
suggested_refs: The Jiangnan river cities of the Yuan

stops.name: Yangzhou, onto the Grand Canal
stops.date_confidence: Place attested in Treccani's reconstruction; the year orders the segment. Treccani notes Yangzhou's later and disputed association with Marco Polo's supposed governorship, an association this file does not carry as fact.
stops.campa: At Yangzhou he joins the Grand Canal and goes north on it, through a system of locks and haulage that moves the empire's grain a thousand miles inland without a wheel turning. He notes the religious houses of the city. The canal is the last stretch of the outward journey; from here the boats run to the capital. Six years out of a river town in Friuli, he is going north on state water, among the grain barges, at the pace of the men on the haulage.
suggested_refs: The Grand Canal grain transport system of the Yuan

stops.name: Khanbaliq, the palace of the Great Khan
stops.date_confidence: The palace chapter is attested (Yule-Cordier ch. 37). The year is an ordering device: Treccani dates the Khanbaliq residence to a presumed 1322-1325, English Wikipedia to three years somewhere between early 1323 and late 1328, and the two ranges cannot be reconciled from the sources reached. Canonical corpus pin for Khanbaliq, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: Cambalec. He describes the palace: a hill raised by hand and planted with trees, a lake dug out beside it, a jar of jade in the hall large enough to hold drink for the whole court, peacocks of gold that beat their wings when they are struck. He describes the banquets seated by rank, the hunts, the standing guard. This is the chapter that the marvel chapters are read against. Nearly everything he reports of the interior can be matched item by item against Chinese and Persian accounts of the same buildings.
suggested_refs: Yule-Cordier ch. 37 on the Khan's palace at Cambalec
The artificial hill and lake of the Yuan imperial city
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Khanbaliq, three years and an archbishop unnamed
stops.date_confidence: Odoric states three years in the capital; the calendar years are not recoverable. Sources contradict each other and the contradiction is left standing: Treccani states that Odoric met John of Montecorvino, archbishop of Khanbaliq until his death in 1328, while the geography lens of the research pool holds that Montecorvino was likely encountered but is never named in the text. Both cannot be right and neither is discarded here. Montecorvino's 1328 death is secure.
stops.campa: He stays three years, by his own count, in a city where the Latin church has an archbishop. John of Montecorvino came out under Nicholas IV, built churches, baptised converts and translated the psalms into a language of the court, and he dies here in 1328. Treccani says the two men met. The Relatio never names him. What Odoric does report is friars going out along the road with a cross to meet the Great Khan, singing, and being received with reverence. Which friars, and whether their archbishop walked with them, he does not say.
suggested_refs: John of Montecorvino's mission and archbishopric at Khanbaliq, 1294-1328
The letters of John of Montecorvino to the Latin West
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Kansan, through the land of Prester John
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Treccani reports that the return narrative moves through the land of Prester John and a region called Kansan, likely Shaanxi, but the return chapters are arranged topically rather than chronologically and cannot be laid out as a route. The pin is a general one for the Shaanxi loess country and does not mark an identified site. Year orders the segment. The quote is Odoric's own stated duration abroad, from ch. 1; the figure of fourteen and a half years is often used to anchor the 1318-1330 chronology and is disputed by modern scholars.
stops.campa: Going home he goes overland. The narrative crosses into what he calls the land of Prester John, a kingdom Latin Europe has been addressing letters to for a century and a half and has never once located on a road. Then a region he calls Kansan, commonly read as Shaanxi, with felt tents and the customs of the people in them. The return chapters are arranged by subject and not by route. Where he was in which year on the way home is not recoverable from the text, and Treccani does not attempt it.
stops.quote: Fourteen years and a half, in the habit of Francis, that blessed confessor of Christ, I sojourned in those parts of the world.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Friar Odoric, ch. 1, Yule-Cordier trans., Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II, p. 98
suggested_refs: The Prester John legend in the Latin West, twelfth to fourteenth century

stops.name: Tibet, the skull made a cup
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and disputed. Older reference works made Odoric the first European to enter Lhasa on the strength of this chapter; the text does not securely name Lhasa, and modern scholarship treats his presence there as plausible but unproved, allowing that some of the material may be reported rather than seen. The pin is Lhasa, used for want of any other, and should be read with that caution. Year orders the segment.
stops.campa: He reports a country called Tibet: felt tents, a religious superior he compares to a pope, and a funeral in which the dead are cut apart and the skull is made into a drinking vessel for the family to use. Older reference books made him the first European into Lhasa on the strength of this chapter alone. The text does not name Lhasa. Modern scholarship calls his presence there possible and unproved, and allows that parts of the chapter may be things he was told on the road rather than things he watched.
suggested_refs: The disputed claim of Odoric as the first European in Lhasa

stops.name: Padua, the report taken down by William of Solagna
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month by Treccani and by William of Solagna's own colophon, which dates the dictation to May 1330 at the house of St Anthony in Padua. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates: the research pool's two lenses gave 45.4009, 11.8767 and 45.3999, 11.8827 for the same house; the latter is used, being within about 150 m of the Basilica of St Anthony, and the discrepancy is flagged rather than resolved.
stops.campa: In May, at the Franciscan house beside the tomb of Anthony, the provincial minister Guidotto orders him to make a report, and Friar William of Solagna takes it down. Solagna's colophon says he wrote it as Odoric spoke it and did not attempt an ornate Latin. Twelve years of walking come out as fifty short chapters in a plain hand. No commissioning document survives. Nobody knows whether the report was meant for the archive at Padua, for the provincial chapter, or for the papal court at Avignon.
stops.quote: And now being at Padua, I have here compiled this little work at the request of the reverend Friar Guidotto, the minister of the province of Saint Anthony. If, then, the studious reader shall find anything good in it, let him ascribe that to the divine bounty and not to my poor skill. And if he find anything too hard for belief, and wherein he judgeth me to stray from truth, let him remark thereon with a student's charity, and not with insolent bitterness and spiteful snarling.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Friar Odoric, ch. 1 (closing dictation note), Yule-Cordier trans., Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II, p. 98
suggested_refs: William of Solagna's colophon dating the dictation to May 1330
Annalia Marchisio, 'Many Versions, One Edition,' Journal of Medieval Latin 26 (2016)
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Padua, the sworn attestation
stops.date_confidence: Attested text, uncertain placement. Yule prints the attestation as ch. 50 following the Farsetti and Bollandist versions, and footnotes that no single manuscript has this arrangement; the passage occupies pp. 266-267, not p. 267 as the research pool gave it. Solagna's colophon dates the whole dictation to May 1330, so the pool's note placing the attestation shortly before Odoric's death in 1331 is wrong.
stops.campa: He swears to it. Under obedience, to Guidotto, he declares that everything written down he either saw with his own eyes or had from men worthy of credit, and that where he did not see, the common talk of those countries bears witness. Then he says he has left things out: things he judged would be thought too hard for belief by men who had not seen them. A book with dog-faced men in it contains a further set of marvels that its own author suppressed as implausible. Nobody knows what those were.
stops.quote: I, Friar Odoric the Bohemian of Friuli, from a certain town called Pordenone, of the Order of Minorites and the Province of St. Anthony, do solemnly declare and attest to my reverend father the Friar Guidotto, the Minister of the Province aforesaid of St. Anthony in the March of Treviso, in accordance with my vow of obedience and the injunction which he hath laid upon me, that all these things hereinbefore written I either beheld with mine own eyes or heard from men worthy of credit.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Friar Odoric, ch. 50 (final attestation), Yule-Cordier trans., Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II, pp. 266-267
suggested_refs: Yule-Cordier ch. 50 and the editor's note on the attestation's manuscript placement
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), archive.org

stops.name: Pisa, the ship for Avignon not taken
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, not documented fact. The journey toward Pisa, the intention of sailing to Avignon for missionary reinforcements, and the dream of Francis ordering him back to his nest all come from later Franciscan hagiography (Wadding, Mark of Lisbon) as characterised by Tilatti. No contemporary document supports any of it. The month is an ordering device placing the attempt after the May dictation and before the January death.
stops.campa: Tradition sends him out from Padua toward Pisa, to take ship for Avignon and ask the pope in person for more men for the eastern mission. He gets as far as Pisa and falls ill. A dream of Francis is later said to have turned him back, ordering him home to his nest. None of this stands in a contemporary document; it comes from Wadding and Mark of Lisbon, writing centuries afterward, and Tilatti presents it as tradition and nothing firmer. What is certain is that he never reached Avignon and that he went back to Friuli.
stops.quote: But, as for me, from day to day I prepare myself to return to those countries in which I am content to die, if so it pleaseth Him from whom all good things do come.
stops.quote_source: The Travels of Friar Odoric, ch. 50 (final attestation), dictated at Padua in May 1330; Yule-Cordier trans., Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II, pp. 266-267
suggested_refs: Luke Wadding's Annales Minorum and Mark of Lisbon's chronicle on the Avignon attempt

segments.name: Udine, the Body and the Cult

stops.name: Udine, death at San Francesco
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Treccani: Monday, 14 January 1331, at the Franciscan convent of San Francesco, Udine. The weekday checks out against the Julian calendar. Two details in the research pool could not be confirmed in the Treccani text reached and are omitted from the campa: the named magistrate Conrad Bernardiggi and the crowd cutting at the habit and hair. Coordinates corrected to 46.0608, 13.2358, the church in Borgo Grazzano; the pool gave three different Udine pairs for the same building.
stops.campa: He dies at the convent of San Francesco in Udine on a Monday in January, about fifty years old, some seven months after dictating the book. The friars intend a quiet burial the same day. Udine does not permit it: the town takes the funeral over, and reports of healing at the body begin at once. James of Ireland, who walked beside him on the road, enters the surviving record exactly once, on the fifth of April, when the commune pays him two marks amore Dei et Odorici, for the love of God and of Odoric.
suggested_refs: The public financial records of Udine, payment of 5 April 1331 to Friar James of Ireland
The church of San Francesco, Borgo Grazzano, Udine
sources: Yule and Cordier, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. II (1913), citing the public records of Udine, archive.org

stops.name: Udine, the seventy miracles and the twenty-seven
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month by Treccani: in May 1331 the Patriarch of Aquileia, Pagano della Torre, appointed a canon and a notary to take sworn testimony on reported healings at the tomb. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. The named officials (Melioranzi, Maffeo Cassini, the notary Guecelli) and the seventy-versus-twenty-seven discrepancy come from the geography lens of the research pool citing Tilatti.
stops.campa: In May the Patriarch of Aquileia, Pagano della Torre, appoints a canon and a notary to take sworn testimony on what is happening at the tomb. The document is built exactly like a canonization inquiry and it is not one: no completed papal proceeding from that year survives, only this patriarchal file, sworn and notarised in a Friulian town. The heading of the process advertises seventy miracles. The record enumerates twenty-seven. Nobody has explained the other forty-three.
suggested_refs: The 1331 sworn miracle inquiry of Patriarch Pagano della Torre

stops.name: Udine, the stone sarcophagus
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year by Treccani, which dates the commission and the elevation to 1332 without a month; the pool's 'May 1332' is unsupported and the month is defaulted to 01. Material corrected: Treccani says a stone sarcophagus, sarcofago di pietra, not alabaster; the pool's two lenses contradicted each other on this and stone is right. The reported presence of Beatrice of Bavaria, Countess of Gorizia, is not in the Treccani text reached and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: The commune of Udine pays for a stone sarcophagus and the Venetian Filippo de Sanctis carves it. Treccani calls it a sarcofago di pietra, stone and not the alabaster that later accounts give it. The body is lifted into it in a ceremony that functions as a local canonization performed by a patriarch: no pope is involved, and nobody in Udine appears to think one is needed for the town to keep its own saint. Eighteen months after the death, the friar who came back from Cathay is lying in public money, carved, where the town can walk past him.
suggested_refs: The sarcophagus of Filippo de Sanctis, commissioned by the commune of Udine, 1332

stops.name: Rome, the cult confirmed ab immemorabili
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Treccani and corroborated by Wikipedia. The formal Roman inquiry into the immemorial cult opened in 1749. Odoric was of course never in Rome; the stop is placed here because the act is the disposition of his own cult and belongs to no other subject.
stops.campa: Four hundred and twenty-four years after the funeral, Benedict XIV confirms the cult ab immemorabili: a ruling that the veneration is so old its beginning cannot be traced, commonly described as equipollent beatification. It ratifies what Udine did in 1332 and stops short of canonization. A formal Roman inquiry into the immemorial cult had opened six years before. Odoric is beato, and beato is what he has stayed; the diocesan phase reopened in 2002 closed positively in 2006 and the papers went to Rome, where they are.
suggested_refs: Benedict XIV's confirmation of the cult, 2 July 1755
The Bollandist Acta Sanctorum for 14 January, Antwerp 1643

stops.name: Santa Maria del Carmine, the relics moved
stops.date_confidence: Date corrected: Italian Wikipedia dates the transfer to the former Carmelite church to 1771, while 1769 is the year of the Venetian suppression of the religious houses; the research pool blurred the two into '1769-71'. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinates corrected to 46.0587, 13.2431, the Chiesa della Beata Vergine del Carmine on Via Aquileia, per Nominatim; the pool gave two other pairs, both roughly a kilometre off.
stops.campa: The Venetian suppression closes the Franciscan house, and the relics and the sarcophagus are carried across Udine with civic and ecclesiastical ceremony to the former Carmelite church on the Borgo Aquileia. They are still there. In 2002, on the anniversary of the death, the diocese opened the ark and examined what was inside: a partly mummified body, a man of about fifty, dead of cardiac complications with respiratory insufficiency. The birth year now rests on that examination and on nothing written down at the time.
suggested_refs: The Chiesa della Beata Vergine del Carmine, Via Aquileia, Udine
The 2002 diocesan examination of the remains

stops.name: Pordenone, the monument, the church, the asteroid
stops.date_confidence: Composite stop at the home pin, dated to the earliest of the three commemorations. The 1881 monument and the 1992 Mario Botta church are attested by the Wikipedia articles; asteroid 4637 Odorico was discovered at Chions, in the province of Pordenone, on 8 February 1989 by J. M. Baur, per the Minor Planet Center, whose naming citation prints the superseded birth year 1265. Month and day for the monument are unknown and defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The town he is named for takes centuries to claim him and then does it thoroughly. A public monument goes up in 1881. In 1992 a parish church designed by Mario Botta is finished and dedicated to him, brick and drum and a slot of light. Three years before that, from an observatory at Chions in the same province, an asteroid was found on 8 February 1989 and named 4637 Odorico. Its citation in the Minor Planet Center's register still prints his dates as 1265 to 1331.
suggested_refs: The 1881 monument to Odoric at Pordenone
Mario Botta's church of the Beato Odorico, Pordenone, 1992
Minor Planet Center citation for 4637 Odorico, discovered at Chions, 8 February 1989
sources: Minor Planet Center authority record for 4637 Odorico
